# Fetal growth restriction

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Obstetrics/gynecology > Pregnancy-associated disorders > Fetal growth restriction*

[Original Article Link](/library/al0QvT)

---

## Summary

Fetal growth restriction (FGR), also known as intrauterine growth restriction, is defined as estimated fetal weight or abdominal circumference below the 10<sup>th</sup> <u>percentile</u> for a given <u>gestational age</u>. FGR is a pathological condition caused by an underlying maternal (e.g., substance use), <u>placental</u> (e.g., <u>placental insufficiency</u>), or fetal factor (e.g., <u>aneuploidy</u>) that impedes the fetus from reaching its expected growth potential, unlike a <u>constitutionally small fetus</u>. All pregnant individuals should be screened for FGR with <u>fundal height</u> measurements from 24 weeks' <u>gestation</u>. <u>Obstetric ultrasound</u> is indicated if <u>fundal height</u> is more than 3 cm below the expected size for <u>gestational age</u>. Further studies may be required to identify the underlying cause of FGR. Management involves treatment of the underlying cause and referral to <u>maternal-fetal medicine</u> for antepartum surveillance and delivery planning.

---

## Etiology

### Maternal causes




* Substance use (e.g., <u>alcohol</u>, cigarettes, <u>cocaine</u>, <u>heroin</u>)

* <u>Teratogenic drugs</u>: <u>ACE inhibitors</u>, <u>carbamazepine</u>, <u>phenytoin</u>, <u>warfarin</u>

* <u>Maternal phenylketonuria</u>

* Systemic diseases resulting in <u>placental insufficiency</u>





### Uteroplacental causes




* Placental insufficiency (most common cause in the US) [[1]](/library/uE1pxi0)

* Definition: A disorder of the fetomaternal circulation that causes inadequate blood flow to the <u>placenta</u> and impaired substance exchange (e.g., oxygen) between the mother and fetus, leading to metabolic compromise of the fetus.

* Causes and <u>risk factors</u>

* Maternal conditions (smoking during <u>pregnancy</u>, <u>diabetes mellitus</u> with vasculopathy, chronic <u>hypertension</u>, <u>severe anemia</u>, <u>anorexia nervosa</u>, <u>antiphospholipid syndrome</u>, <u>SLE</u>, <u>sickle cell disease</u>)

* <u>Pregnancy</u>-related conditions (<u>preeclampsia</u>, <u>Rh incompatibility</u>)

* Clinical features: depend on the underlying cause

* Complications: fetal growth restriction, <u>placental abruption</u>, <u>preterm labor</u>, <u>stillbirth</u>, <u>Potter sequence</u>, <u>oligohydramnios</u>

* <u>Placenta previa</u>

* <u>Multiple gestation</u>

* <u>Placental abruption</u>

* <u>Umbilical artery</u> <u>thrombosis</u>/extensive <u>infarction</u> [[5]](/library/-5YD5p)

* Uterine <u>malformations</u> (e.g., <u>fibroids</u>)





### Fetal factors




* Genetic abnormalities in the fetus (e.g., <u>aneuploidy</u>)

* <u>Cyanotic congenital heart defects</u>

* Early intrauterine infections (<u>TORCH</u>)





> [!TIP]
> Asymmetrical fetal growth restriction is the most common manifestation of fetal growth restriction (∼ 70%), has a late onset, and is usually due to maternal systemic disease (e.g., <u>hypertension</u>) that results in <u>placental insufficiency</u>. Symmetrical fetal growth restriction is less common (∼ 30%) and is usually due to a genetic disorder (e.g., <u>aneuploidy</u>), <u>congenital heart disease</u>, or early intrauterine <u>TORCH infection</u> that affects the fetus early in <u>gestation</u>.

---

## Pathophysiology

Recent studies show that the symmetry of growth restriction alone cannot reliably indicate an intrinsic or extrinsic cause; therefore, the terms “symmetrical” and “asymmetrical” FGR should be avoided. Symmetrical and asymmetrical FGR are covered in this article for exam purposes. [[7]](/library/lK1vg30)




### Asymmetrical fetal growth restriction




* The head is normally proportioned while the body and limbs are thin and small.

* Caused by extrinsic factors, which affect the fetus in the later stages of <u>gestation</u> (i.e., <u>third trimester</u>).

* Impaired function of the uteroplacental unit (see <u>placental function</u>) → insufficient transplacental delivery of oxygen and <u>nutrients</u> to the fetus and impaired return of carbon dioxide and fetal metabolic waste products from the fetus to the mother's circulation

* Effect on <u>fetal development</u>

* Fetal <u>hypoxia</u> and <u>hypoglycemia</u> → shunting of blood flow to vital fetal organs (<u>brain</u>, <u>heart</u>, and <u>adrenal glands</u>) bypassing other organs (e.g., <u>liver</u>, muscle, <u>fat tissue</u>)

* Fetal switch to <u>anaerobic glycolysis</u> → <u>metabolic acidosis</u> → <u>lactic acid</u> accumulates → progressive damage to vital fetal organs (e.g., <u>brain</u>, <u>myocardium</u>) → permanent damage, possibly fetal <u>death</u>

* Effect on maternal factors

* Decreased <u>placental</u> growth (↓ <u>placental</u> surface area) → further impairs <u>placental function</u>

* ↑ Risk of <u>preeclampsia</u>, <u>preterm labor</u>, <u>vaginal bleeding</u> [[8]](/library/Yuanpm)





### Symmetrical fetal growth restriction




* <u>Global</u> growth restriction, affecting all parts of the body

* Caused by intrinsic factors (e.g., genetic abnormalities, infections), which affect the fetus in the early stages of <u>gestation</u>.

---

## Clinical features

### Fetal signs




* Decreased or absent fetal movements [[9]](/library/0_ae5M)

* At <u>birth</u>: <u>small for gestational age</u> (<u>birth</u> weight below 10<sup>th</sup> <u>percentile</u>)





### Maternal signs




* Mostly asymptomatic

* Decreased <u>symphysis-fundal height</u> 

* Measured between 24 and 36 weeks of <u>gestation</u>  [[10]](/library/MYcMpa0)

* <u>Fundal height</u> at least 3 cm less than <u>gestational age</u> in weeks is a sign of FGR.

* Small <u>uterus</u> (e.g., a smaller abdomen than in previous <u>pregnancies</u>)

* Symptoms of underlying etiology of FGR (e.g., <u>vaginal bleeding</u> secondary to <u>placental abruption</u>)

## Diagnosis

FGR is usually discovered as part of routine <u>prenatal care</u> (e.g., if <u>fundal height</u> is smaller than expected for <u>gestation</u>).




### Approach [[11]](/library/1Kd22I0)[[12]](/library/MPdM2J0)




* Obtain an <u>obstetric ultrasound</u> if:

* <u>Fundal height</u> is more than 3 cm below expected size for <u>gestational age</u> after 24 weeks' <u>gestation</u>

* A <u>risk factor for FGR</u> has been identified [[12]](/library/MPdM2J0)

* Assess for underlying etiologies (e.g., <u>screening for hypertensive pregnancy disorders</u>).

* Determine if FGR is early or late.

* Early-onset FGR: < 32 weeks' <u>gestation</u>

* Late-onset FGR: ≥ 32 weeks' <u>gestation</u>

* Refer to <u>maternal-fetal medicine</u> for advanced diagnostic studies.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Preeclampsia</u> and genetic disorders are common underlying causes of <u>early-onset FGR</u>; a more comprehensive workup is recommended in <u>early-onset FGR</u> than <u>late-onset FGR</u>. [[11]](/library/1Kd22I0)[[12]](/library/MPdM2J0)




### Initial <u>ultrasound</u>




* Finding: estimated fetal weight or abdominal circumference < 10<sup>th</sup> <u>percentile</u> for <u>gestational age</u> [[12]](/library/MPdM2J0)[[13]](/library/Au1RFi0)

* Growth restriction may be: [[14]](/library/hKdcTI0)

* Disproportionate: head is normal size but body and limbs are thin and small

* Proportionate: the entire body is proportionally small

* Manifestations of underlying causes (e.g., fetal anomalies secondary to <u>aneuploidy</u>, signs of <u>placental insufficiency</u>) may be visible.





### Advanced diagnostic studies [[11]](/library/1Kd22I0)




* All patients: detailed <u>obstetric ultrasound</u>

* Perform <u>invasive prenatal genetic testing</u> (and <u>CMV</u> <u>PCR</u> if <u>amniocentesis</u> is performed) for patients with:

* <u>Early-onset FGR</u>

* <u>Polyhydramnios</u>

* Fetal anomalies detected on <u>ultrasound</u>

---

## Differential diagnoses

### Constitutionally small fetus




* Definition: estimated fetal weight < 10<sup>th</sup> <u>percentile</u> without an identified underlying condition

* Predisposing factors [[15]](/library/zgWrBk0)

* Low maternal height

* Low maternal weight before/in early <u>pregnancy</u>

* Asian descent [[16]](/library/iRWJ5O0)

* <u>Parity</u>

* Fetal female sex

* Diagnosis

* Assessment of fetal growth using customized growth charts [[17]](/library/AgWRBk0)

* <u>Doppler velocimetry of the umbilical artery</u>: normal systolic/<u>diastolic</u> <u>ratio</u> [[18]](/library/_gW5Bk0)

* Prognosis: constitutionally small fetuses are not at increased risk for adverse <u>perinatal</u> outcomes





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Management

Start treating underlying <u>causes of FGR</u> (e.g., <u>hypertensive pregnancy disorders</u>, <u>diabetes in pregnancy</u>) and refer patients to <u>maternal-fetal medicine</u> for further management. [[1]](/library/uE1pxi0)[[12]](/library/MPdM2J0)




### Fetal monitoring [[11]](/library/1Kd22I0)[[19]](/library/IE1YCi0)[[20]](/library/ME1Mwi0)




* Initiate <u>antepartum fetal surveillance</u> once the fetus is viable.

* The modality and frequency varies based on maternal and fetal factors, but usually includes:   [[11]](/library/1Kd22I0)[[12]](/library/MPdM2J0)[[19]](/library/IE1YCi0)[[21]](/library/ciWaqO0)

* <u>Ultrasound</u> for fetal growth (<u>fetal biometric parameters</u>)   [[19]](/library/IE1YCi0)

* <u>Doppler velocimetry of the umbilical artery</u> to evaluate for <u>placental insufficiency</u>

* Assesses for reduced, absent, or reversed end-<u>diastolic</u> flow

* Results determine the frequency of repeat monitoring, <u>cardiotocography</u>, and delivery.

* <u>Biophysical profile</u> (<u>BPP</u>) or <u>modified BPP</u> (often including a <u>nonstress test</u>)

* <u>Cardiotocography</u>





### Delivery planning [[11]](/library/1Kd22I0)[[19]](/library/IE1YCi0)




* Immediate delivery if there are signs of <u>fetal distress</u> (e.g., <u>BPP</u> score ≤ 4, repetitive <u>late decelerations</u>)

* Consideration of early scheduled delivery

* Timing of delivery is based on results of <u>Doppler velocimetry of the umbilical artery</u>.   [[11]](/library/1Kd22I0)

* Give <u>antenatal corticosteroid therapy for fetal maturation</u> if delivery is scheduled for < 34 weeks' <u>gestation</u>. [[11]](/library/1Kd22I0)[[12]](/library/MPdM2J0)

## Complications

* <u>Stillbirth</u>

* <u>Preterm labor</u>

* <u>Low birth weight</u>;  (< 2500 g) with ↑ risk of <u>sudden infant death syndrome</u>

* <u>Perinatal asphyxia</u>

* <u>Hypoglycemia</u>, <u>hypocalcemia</u>

* <u>Hypothermia</u>

* Possibly motor and neurological disabilities





> [!WARNING]
> The risk of <u>morbidity</u> and mortality increases in <u>pregnancies</u> affected by <u>early-onset FGR</u>. [[12]](/library/MPdM2J0)




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
